subject: Social Science
source: Based on the opening chapter in the uploaded Class 6 Exploring Society: India and Beyond PDF (fees101.pdf), Reprint 2026–27. This guide uses original explanations and examples.
goals: Explain what social science studies and why it uses questions and evidence.
Distinguish history, geography, civics/political science and economics by the kinds of questions they ask.
Connect people, places, institutions and resources in a single situation.
Use observation and sources to build a careful explanation.
Recognise that social science helps us understand both continuity and change.
summary: Social science helps us understand people and the societies they build. It studies how people live in places, how communities change over time, how decisions are made, how rules and institutions work, and how resources are used. Its branches ask different but connected questions; together they give a fuller picture of everyday life.

concepts.title: A connected study of society
concepts.explanation: A road, a market, a river or a school can be studied from several viewpoints. Geography asks about location and environment; history asks how it developed; civics asks who makes decisions and under which rules; economics asks how people use resources and make choices.
concepts.example: To study a local market, map where it is, find out how it began, identify the rules that affect it, and examine how sellers and buyers decide what to exchange.

concepts.title: History: change over time
concepts.explanation: History investigates past people, events and ways of life using sources such as documents, objects, buildings, inscriptions, photographs and oral accounts. A source must be interpreted in context; one source rarely answers every question.
concepts.example: An old photograph may show the appearance of a street at one time. Comparing it with newer photographs can reveal change, but other sources may be needed to explain why the change happened.

concepts.title: Geography: places and relationships
concepts.explanation: Geography studies the Earth, places, environments and relationships between people and their surroundings. Maps, field observations, photographs and measurements can help describe patterns and connections.
concepts.example: A settlement near a river may use the river for water and transport, while also needing to plan for floods. Geography considers both the benefits and risks of the location.

concepts.title: Civics: rules, rights and public decisions
concepts.explanation: Civics examines how communities organise public life, how decisions are made, what institutions do, and how rights and responsibilities shape relationships between people and government.
concepts.example: If a neighbourhood needs a safe crossing near a school, questions include which local authority is responsible, how residents can raise the issue, and how a decision is implemented.

concepts.title: Economics: choices and resources
concepts.explanation: Economics studies how people make choices when time, money, materials and other resources are limited. It asks how goods and services are produced, shared and used.
concepts.example: A family with a limited budget must prioritise among different needs. A town with limited funds must also choose which public improvements to make first.

concepts.title: Sources, evidence and perspective
concepts.explanation: Social scientists compare sources, ask who created them and why, and check whether different accounts agree. People can experience the same event differently, so careful study considers evidence and perspective together.
concepts.example: A shopkeeper and a customer may describe a price increase differently. Sales records, price changes and other accounts can help explain the situation more fully.

visual.title: Four connected lenses
steps: Civics — who decides and under what rules?

workedExamples.question: A new bridge is built in a village. Frame one question for each of four social-science lenses.
steps: History: What transport routes existed before the bridge?
Geography: How does the river and surrounding land affect the bridge’s location?
Civics: Which public body approved and maintains it?
Economics: How might the bridge change travel costs, trade or access to work?
workedExamples.answer: Each question studies the same bridge from a different but complementary perspective.

workedExamples.question: A single old map shows that a town had fewer streets. Can we conclude why the town grew?
steps: The map is evidence of the street pattern at a particular time.
It does not by itself explain the cause of growth.
Compare maps from different dates and consult other sources such as records, photographs or oral histories.
Separate what the sources show from the explanation inferred from them.
workedExamples.answer: No. The map shows a pattern, but explaining why the town grew requires additional evidence.

practice.question: Why is social science useful in everyday life?
practice.answer: It helps us understand communities, places, public decisions, historical change and resource choices, so we can reason about issues rather than rely only on assumptions.
practice.why: Social science links evidence to how people and societies function.

practice.question: Name two sources that could help investigate the history of a local building.
practice.answer: Examples include old photographs, building records, inscriptions, maps, newspapers, oral accounts or the building itself.
practice.why: Different sources provide different kinds of evidence and should be compared.

practice.question: A town has limited money for a library or a sports ground. Which branch studies the resource-choice problem most directly?
practice.answer: Economics studies the choice and use of limited resources. Civics also helps explain how a public decision should be made.
practice.why: Real issues often require more than one social-science perspective.

practice.question: What is the difference between a source and a conclusion?
practice.answer: A source is material or testimony that provides evidence; a conclusion is an explanation reached after evaluating evidence.
practice.why: The conclusion should not claim more than the sources support.

mcqs.q: Which question is most directly geographical?
options: Who ruled the region 500 years ago?
Where is the settlement and how does the river affect it?
Which law assigns the local budget?
mcqs.why: Geography focuses on place, environment and spatial relationships.

mcqs.q: Which source may help investigate the past?
options: An old inscription compared with other evidence
mcqs.why: Inscriptions can be historical sources, but they must be interpreted and compared.
Economics studies choices, production, distribution and use of resources.

mcqs.q: Why can two people describe the same event differently?
options: They may have different experiences or perspectives
One account must always be invented
mcqs.why: Perspective influences an account; sources and context help evaluate it.

mcqs.q: What is the strongest way to explain why a town changed?
options: Compare relevant sources from different times and check possible causes
mcqs.why: Comparing evidence helps distinguish observed change from its possible causes.

revision: Social science studies people, places, communities, institutions and choices.
History asks about the past and change; geography studies places and human-environment relationships.
Civics examines public life, rules, rights and institutions; economics examines choices and resources.
One real-world issue can be studied through several connected lenses.
Sources are evidence; conclusions must be reasoned from evidence and its limitations.

chapterTest.instructions: Use complete sentences and identify the evidence or reasoning behind your answer.

questions.q: Explain why a market can be studied using more than one branch of social science.
questions.answer: Geography can study its location, history can study how it developed, civics can study rules and public services, and economics can study prices, work and exchange.

questions.q: Why should a historian compare more than one source?
questions.answer: Sources may be incomplete or reflect different perspectives. Comparison helps check claims and understand context.

questions.q: Give an example of a public issue that connects civics and economics.
questions.answer: Choosing how a town spends a limited budget connects civics (decision-making and responsibility) with economics (prioritising limited resources).

questions.q: Explain the difference between evidence and inference.
questions.answer: Evidence is information from a source or observation. An inference is a possible explanation drawn from that evidence and must be checked.
